title: Vector-borne disease range expansion forecasting
bottleneck: Warming is pushing malaria, dengue, and other vector-borne diseases into highlands and temperate zones, but forecasting where they will establish is blocked by interacting unknowns: vector adaptation, human immunity, urbanization, and control measures all modulate the climate signal. Surveillance in newly at-risk regions is weak, so emergence is detected only after outbreaks. Health systems in expansion zones lack the diagnostics, drugs, and institutional memory to respond.
why_it_blocks: Disease range expansion threatens hundreds of millions newly exposed with no immunity, overwhelming unprepared health systems. The forecasting gap means prevention arrives after the outbreak instead of before it.
current_state: Climate-informed early warning systems for dengue and malaria are being piloted, and genomic surveillance tracks vector spread. But operational, localized forecasts that drive preemptive public health action exist in only a handful of places.
